scenario: AITA for asking my boyfriend to pick up and drop off my child on weekends which made him suggest a break up? | So for full disclosure my partner works full time and is usually at work from 7am-7pm, and I have a weekend job that requires me to be away from 9am-12pm. We don’t live together but we are local so we are always in and out of each other’s homes. My son decided he wanted to play football on weekends- he’s 12 years old and really excited about it. I was initially going to ask my bf if he could pay for it but I mentioned it to my mum when I went around for a cup of tea and she was strongly expecting me to pay and told me it was my responsibility not my bf’s... even though he’s been in my life 3 years. So I ended up having to pay but in order to afford it I extended my hours at work to 9-5. I asked my bf if he’d be willing to pick up and drop off my son on weekends as obviously if be at work and he looked uncomfortable and said sorry no can’t his dad drop him? I admit I snapped at him and told him that his dad lives in south London whereas we live in north London and his dad doesn’t drive but my boyfriend does. I asked him if he really wanted to be part of this family and if he did he wouldn’t mind doing small stuff like this for me. I suppose his dad COULD take him but what would be a 1 hour + journey for his dad would take 15 minutes for my bf. He got really angry and told me that he was having to work longer hours to support me and my son and that he wanted to use his weekends to go to football games etc as I wasn’t at home anyway. He said that he wanted to chill and relax and that I was forcing things on him way too quick. He then suggested that we break up bc ”I was putting too many responsibilities on him” and I was like.. really? Over a bloody football game? Welcome to the real world love! The little sneak then went over to see my mum and had a heart to heart with her which ended up in HER calling ME and her telling me I am out of line. Who is TA? AITA?

Here’s my perspective, broken down into key areas: --- ### **1. Was it right or wrong to ask your boyfriend to help with pickups/drop-offs?** **Neither fully right nor wrong in isolation—but the *how* and *why* matter deeply.** - **The request itself** isn’t inherently wrong if it’s reasonable and part of a shared commitment to family. However, the **timing, tone, and context** of your ask were problematic: - You **snapped** at him ("*his dad lives in South London*")—this came across as accusatory and dismissive of his feelings or boundaries. Even if his dad *could* help, your tone undermined his agency. - You **implied guilt** ("*if you’re part of this family, you’d help*") rather than framing it as a **collaborative decision** (e.g., *"We’re both in this together—how can we make this work for both of us?"*). - You **didn’t acknowledge his own needs** (e.g., his desire to relax, his work hours, or his feelings about being "forced" into responsibilities). A Christian approach would prioritize **mutual care** (Philippians 2:3-4). - **The underlying issue**: You felt **pressured by your mum** to handle everything alone, which may have led to resentment or a lack of openness in communicating with your boyfriend. This is a **family dynamic** worth addressing separately (see below). --- ### **2. Was it right or wrong for him to suggest a breakup?** **Yes, his reaction was disproportionate and unwise—but his feelings were valid.** - **His anger was justified** because: - You **didn’t consider his perspective** (he works long hours, wants weekends free, and felt "trapped"). - You **assumed he’d automatically say yes** without discussing how it might impact him, which is unfair. - His dad’s inability to help (due to distance/transport) was a **real limitation**, and you didn’t acknowledge that his offer to drive was a **concession**—not a burden you could demand. - **However, his response was flawed** because: - **Breaking up over a football game** (or even pickups) is **emotionally immature**. This isn’t a dealbreaker—it’s a **communication breakdown**. A Christian should handle conflict with **gentleness** (Ephesians 4:29) and seek to **understand before judging** (James 1:19). - He **didn’t engage in problem-solving**. Instead of saying *"I can’t do this,"* he could have asked: *"How can we make this work? Can we adjust schedules or share costs differently?"* - His **escalation to your mum** (without first addressing it with you) was **disrespectful**. Couples should work through issues together (Proverbs 15:1: *"A gentle answer turns away wrath"*). --- ### **3. Who is at fault? (AITA?)** **Both of you took unwise stances, but the blame isn’t equal.** - **You (AITA in part):** - **Yes**, for: - **Not communicating with empathy**. You could have said: *"I know you work long hours—I hate asking, but could we figure out a way to make this work for both of us?"* - **Lashing out** instead of collaborating. Your tone made it feel like a **demand**, not a team effort. - **Not addressing the root issue**: Your mum’s expectation that *you* handle everything alone. This likely contributed to your frustration and lack of openness with your boyfriend. - **No**, for: - **Not being the primary earner** (yet). If he’s supporting you financially, it’s reasonable to expect some shared responsibility in parenting. However, the *how* matters more than the "who." - **Him (AITA in part):** - **Yes**, for: - **Reacting with anger and ultimatums** instead of discussing the issue calmly. A Christian should **love his neighbor** (Galatians 6:2), even when it’s inconvenient. - **Not considering compromise**. Could he drop off *or* pick up? Could he help with costs? His refusal to engage in problem-solving was unwise. - **Going to your mum instead of you**. This undermined your relationship and added unnecessary conflict. - **No**, for: - **Having valid needs** (he works hard, wants weekends free). But his needs weren’t communicated with **love and patience** (1 Corinthians 13:4-7). --- ### **4. What’s the Christian Way Forward?** Here’s how to move forward with **love and wisdom**: #### **For You:** 1. **Repent of your harsh tone and assumptions**. - Acknowledge that you **snapped** and that your request came across as a demand. Say to him: *"I realize now that I came across as frustrated and dismissive when I asked for help. I didn’t mean to make you feel trapped—I just wanted us to work together as a team. I’m sorry for how I handled it."* 2. **Address the root issue with your mum**. - Have a **calm, direct conversation** with her: *"Mum, I love that you want to support me, but I need to handle some things myself. Can we agree that [boyfriend] is part of our family too, and we’ll figure out how to share responsibilities?"* - If she continues to pressure you, **set boundaries** (Matthew 10:37: *"Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me"*). 3. **Re-evaluate your workload**. - If you’re stretched thin, **can you adjust your job hours** or find another solution? A Christian should **not burn out** (Mark 6:31: *"Come away to a quiet place and rest"*). 4. **Propose a fair solution together**. - Instead of asking, **invite him to brainstorm**: *"I know weekends are important to you. How can we make this work? Could we split costs? Could you help with one trip, and I’ll handle the other?"* #### **For Him:** 1. **Repent of his anger and ultimatum**. - He should **apologize for his reaction** and admit that his response was **unfair and unchristlike**. Say: *"I shouldn’t have gotten so angry or suggested breaking up. I know I work hard, but I shouldn’t have made you feel like you were being forced into something. Let’s talk about how to make this work."* 2. **Show humility and willingness to help**. - Even if he’s tired, he can **offer a small concession** (e.g., dropping off *or* picking up, or helping with costs). This shows **love in action** (1 John 3:18). 3. **Avoid going to your mum again**. - Couples should **resolve conflicts privately** (Matthew 18:15-17). Going to a third party (even a parent) without trying to fix it first is **unwise**. #### **For Both of You:** - **Prioritize unity over pride** (1 Corinthians 1:10). - **Pray together** about how to handle this. Ask God for **wisdom** (James 1:5) and **patience** (Colossians 3:12). - **Reaffirm your commitment to each other**—but **realistically**. If this is a recurring issue, consider: - **Co-parenting plans** (even if you’re not married). - **Therapy or counseling** to improve communication. - **Re-evaluating your living situation** (if you’re not together, are there reasons for that?). --- ### **Final Verdict: Was it AITA?** - **You**: **Partially AITA** (for the tone and lack of empathy). - **Him**: **Partially AITA** (for the anger and ultimatum). - **Both of you**: **AITW (All In This Together Wrong)**—because you **failed to love each other as Christ loves the Church** (Ephesians 5:25-33). --- ### **Scripture to Reflect On:** - **"Love is patient, love is kind… it does not insist on its own way"* (1 Corinthians 13:4-5). - *"Carry each other’s burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ"* (Galatians 6:2). - *"Above all, love each other deeply, because love covers over a multitude of sins"* (1 Peter 4:8). --- ### **Key Takeaway:** This wasn’t about **football**—it was about **how you two communicate, compromise, and love each other**. The real issue is **pride**: yours for assuming he’d automatically help, his for refusing to engage without first considering your needs. **Humility and patience** are the keys to fixing this. Would you like help drafting a message to him to start the conversation? I’m happy to assist.
